## Getting Set Up
For this activity, you will pair program: two people sharing one keyboard. The handout for this activity has reminders about the two roles.

To start, the person whose first name comes later in the alphabet should be the Computer, and the person whose name comes earlier in the alphabet should be the Navigator.

## Exploring Variables

Choose two of the remaining numerical variables in the dataset to investigate their relationship to `price`. The options are: `bed`, `bath`, `year_built`, and `lot`.

```{code-blanks-response}
What two variables did you choose?
```

You'll make graphs and calculate correlations to see how each of those variables might be related to `price`. Start by making a scatterplot with **one** of your chosen variables as the explanatory variable (x) and `price` as the response variable (y).

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: blank1
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: price
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: blank2
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: blank3
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: blank4
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

ggplot(duke_forest) +
  aes(x = blank1, y = price) +
  geom_point() + 
  labs(
    title = "blank2",
    x = "blank3",
    y = "blank4"
  )

```

```{code-blanks-response}
Describe the relationship in the scatterplot. Is it linear or nonlinear? Strong, moderate, or weak? If it is linear, is it positive or negative?
```

To get a quantitative sense of the relationship, calculate the correlation between your first variable and `price`.

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: blank1
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: price
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

cor(duke_forest$blank1, duke_forest$price, "pairwise.complete.obs")

```

```{code-blanks-response}
Is the value of the correlation what you expected based on the scatterplot? Why or why not?
```

Now do the same with your other variable. First, the scatterplot.


## Simple Linear Regression

**Before starting this section,** switch who is the Computer and who is the Navigator.

Now you'll use the variable you chose at the end of the last section to make a linear regression model for predicting `price`. Fill in the blanks below to make a model with your variable as the explanatory variable and `price` as the response variable.

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: blank1
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: price
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

model1 <- lm(price ~ blank1, duke_forest)
summary(model1)

```

```{code-blanks-response}
What is the equation of the regression line from this model?
```

```{code-blanks-response}
Choose an example value of your explanatory variable. Say that value, and use your model to predict what the price of that house would be.
```

You can also add your regression line into the scatterplot using `geom_smooth()`. Fill in the blanks below.

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: blank1
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: price
#|   prefill: true
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: blank2
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: blank3
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: blank4
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

ggplot(duke_forest) +
  aes(x = blank1, y = price) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = lm, se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "blank2",
    x = "blank3",
    y = "blank4"
  )

```

```{code-blanks-response}
How strong of a fit does the model visually seem to be to the data?
```

**STOP.** Check in with Aidan or Dr. O here.

```{code-blanks-response}
Find the "Multiple R-squared" in the linear regression output. What is this value? Is this what you would expect visually from the scatterplot and regression line, and why or why not?
```

## Multiple Linear Regression

**Before starting this section,** switch who is the Computer and who is the Navigator.

Now you'll make a model using both of the variables you considered as explanatory variables. Fill in the blanks below to make a model with your two variables as explanatory variables and `price` as the response variable.

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: blank1
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: price
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: blank2
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token   

model2 <- lm(price ~ blank1 + blank2, duke_forest)
summary(model2)

```

```{code-blanks-response}
What is the equation of the regression line from this model?
```

```{code-blanks-response}
Choose example value for each of your explanatory variables. Say those two values, and use your model to predict what the price of that house would be.
```

**STOP.** Check in with Aidan or Dr. O here.

```{code-blanks-response}
Find the "Multiple R-squared" in the linear regression output. What is this value? Is it higher or lower than in your simple linear regression model?
```
